query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray stand-off distance by 20–30% will yield a thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat with controlled in-flight oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a particle size distribution of 15–45 μm in its as-received state.
generation.intervention: Decrement the spray stand-off distance from the baseline setting (e.g., from ~120 mm to ~90–100 mm) during the thermal-spray deposition process.
generation.conditions: Deposition using HVOF or APS in a controlled or inert atmosphere with standard substrate preparation at ambient conditions, while monitoring substrate temperature to avoid overheating.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduced distance enhances particle velocity at impact and minimizes in-flight residence time, thereby increasing splat flattening, promoting better layer build-up and deposition efficiency.
generation.mechanism: Higher impact kinetic energy with a shorter in-flight time permits rapid solidification and minimizes oxidation exposure; however, optimal distance must be maintained to avoid substrate overheating or particle rebound that compromises uniformity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The bond coat will be 30–50% thicker than the baseline 15–45 μm range with oxidation levels comparable to or lower than those in standard processing, provided the optimum distance is maintained.
generation.baseline: Standard spray parameters yield a 15–45 μm coating with moderate oxidation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is effective when the reduced distance does not induce substrate overheating or excessive particle rebound; adjustments must remain within the system's industrial parameters.
generation.uncertainty: Excessive reduction in distance may lead to substrate thermal damage or uneven deposition if the particles do not properly flatten, which necessitates careful parameter optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct side-by-side depositions at the standard distance (120 mm) and reduced distances (90–100 mm) while monitoring substrate temperature and spray plume consistency.
measurements: Oxide content via EDS and XRD analysis
Adhesion and uniformity via mechanical and SEM analyses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduced-distance deposit does not show at least a 30% increase in thickness or if increased oxidation and substrate damage are observed compared to the baseline, then reject the hypothesis.

As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. cited_evidence.kind: web:2.3. Atmospheric Plasma Spraying Coating of Samples
cited_evidence.text: Pre-heating of the processed HEA powder was carried out by placing it in the oven for 2 h at 25–150 °C, to remove any moisture present. The substrates were pre-heated with the flame of the spraying gun before the powder feed start. Plasma sprayed samples were manufactured by conventional Atmospheric Plasma Spraying system (Metco 9MC, Sulzer Metco Inc., Westbury, NY, USA) using a stand-off distance of 250 mm. Argon (Ar) gas was employed as the primary plasma operating gas and hydrogen (H2) was used as the secondary gas to escalate the whole plasma jet temperature. The feedstock ball milled powder was conveyed by a separate argon source and inoculated superficially into the spawned plasma jet at an angle of 90° concerning the anode axis. After that plasma torch assembly was mounted onto a robotic arm (YR-SK16-J00 Motoman, Yaskawa Electric Corp, Fukuoka, Japan) to navigate across the substrate holders for coating. papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy (HEA) deposited via HVOF
papers.approach: High-velocity oxygen fuel spraying (HVOF) with variation in spray distance to modulate particle temperature, kinetic energy, and exposure to oxygen in flight
papers.findings: An increase in spray distance led to a slight decrease in coating thickness and an increase in coating porosity and oxide content. The longer particle flight time decreased kinetic energy and enhanced in‐flight oxidation, which also resulted in phase transformations (Al‐depleted BCC transforming to FCC near the surface).
papers.mechanism: Lower kinetic energy at longer distances reduces splat flattening and adhesion, while extended oxygen exposure promotes in-flight oxidation that depletes aluminum from the core, destabilizing the BCC phase.

papers.title: Microstructure and Corrosion Behavior of Atmospheric Plasma Sprayed NiCoCrAlFe High Entropy Alloy Coating.
papers.system: NiCoCrAlFe high-entropy alloy deposited via atmospheric plasma spraying (APS)
papers.approach: APS deposition with attention to process parameters such as stand-off distance, plasma power, and feedstock properties, with subsequent phase and surface microstructure analyses
papers.findings: APS coatings developed a multiphase lamellar microstructure with both BCC and FCC phases and featured varying oxide contents. The sprayed coatings showed higher roughness when sprayed without post-treatment, while annealing modified the phases and improved corrosion resistance.
papers.mechanism: The high plasma jet temperatures produce rapid melting and in-flight oxidation, while the spray distance and velocity control particle temperature, melting state, and subsequent bond formation between splats.

papers.title: Microstructural Evolution of AlCoCrFeNiSi High-Entropy Alloy Powder during Mechanical Alloying and Its Coating Performance.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy used for APS deposition
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying of the feedstock powder to obtain a desired particle size and shape for APS deposition, with a detailed investigation of splat formation, surface morphology, and coating microstructure
papers.findings: Feedstock with optimal particle size and shape (milled for 10 h) yielded good flowability and produced coatings with flattened splat microstructures; however, processing parameters strongly affected the degree of melting, porosity, and surface roughness.
papers.mechanism: Uniform particle melting leads to improved mechanical bonding; fine control of particle kinetic energy and flight dynamics is critical to balancing deposition efficiency against undesired oxidation.

established: Spray parameters such as stand-off distance, particle kinetic energy, and feedstock particle size/distribution critically influence coating thickness, porosity, and oxidation levels in thermal-sprayed high-entropy alloy coatings.
In-flight oxidation can be a double-edged sword: while some oxidation may improve hardness and wear resistance, excessive oxidation compromises coating integrity and alters phase distribution.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying the spraying distance (stand-off distance) during HVOF/APS deposition
approaches_tried.outcome: Longer distances result in increased oxidation and greater particle scattering, lowering deposition efficiency and reducing coating thickness.

approaches_tried.approach: Modifying feedstock powder properties via mechanical alloying to optimize particle size and shape
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved flowability and melting lead to enhanced deposition quality, but does not fully address limitations in deposit thickness for fine feedstock powders (15–45 μm).

mechanisms: Reduced particle kinetic energy at increased spray distances leads to lower impact momentum and decreased splat formation, reducing coating thickness.
Prolonged in-flight residence time increases oxidation, which can alter the alloy’s phase structure and potentially weaken the bond coat if oxidation becomes excessive.
Optimized particle melting and deposition dynamics are essential for obtaining a dense, adherent coating with minimal reactivity during flight.
disagreements: Some studies note that a degree of in-flight oxidation can improve hardness and wear resistance, while others emphasize that even minimal oxidation is undesirable for bond coats in thermal barrier systems.
There is varying emphasis on the trade-off between reducing spray distance (to boost deposition rate and thickness) and the risk of higher thermal loads or substrate damage.
open_questions: Can a process adjustment—specifically a reduction in spray distance—consistently yield a thicker bond coat from a 15–45 μm feedstock without increasing oxidation beyond acceptable limits?
How do changes in spray parameters (e.g., stand-off distance and powder feed rate) interact with the inherent oxidation kinetics of FeCoNiCrAl alloys during deposition?
What are the long-term effects of a modified deposition regime on the bond coat’s adhesion and performance under thermal barrier service conditions?
opportunities: Investigate the single intervention of reducing the spray stand-off distance to increase particle kinetic energy and reduce in-flight oxidation time, potentially leading to thicker coatings.
Combine the reduced distance intervention with optimized powder feed rates and preheating strategies to enhance deposition efficiency while preserving the minimal oxidation state.

directions.assessment: This approach directly boosts particle kinetic energy by shortening the in-flight time, which enhances splat flattening and minimizes the time available for oxidation. The literature (e.g., PMC10820071 and PMC8875499) shows that longer distances lower deposition efficiency and increase oxide content, so a reduction should address both issues effectively.

Encapsulating the spray plume with an inert gas (such as additional argon) can further minimize oxygen exposure. This allows for process adjustments (including a shorter spray distance) without increasing oxidation. The idea is supported by studies discussing control of in-flight oxidation (e.g., PMC10820071), though integration complexity must be considered.

Preheating the feedstock can improve particle melting and reduce thermal shock, leading to enhanced splat formation and deposition efficiency. Prior evidence from studies on powder morphology (e.g., PMC5849017) suggests that optimally preheated powders yield better flowability and coating quality, which may also help to overcome the thickness shortfall.

Raising the powder feed rate increases the amount of material delivered per unit time, potentially resulting in a thicker deposit. This intervention, while keeping other parameters constant, is supported by process optimization studies (e.g., PMC11857518) and targets the shortfall in coating build-up, albeit with careful control to avoid issues like agglomeration.

Refining the particle size distribution within the existing 15–45 μm range may improve melting uniformity and deposition dynamics. However, this approach is constrained by the available feedstock and might alter spray dynamics in less predictable ways.
